The End of “May Contain” Confusion? Experts Propose New Food Allergy Labeling Rules

By Dave Bloom

-

2026/10/14
47

    Instaread

    Food labels warning that a product “may contain” peanuts, milk, or other allergens are a familiar sight, but they often leave shoppers guessing. Because these warnings are largely voluntary and unregulated, food companies sometimes use them to protect themselves from lawsuits, even when the likelihood of contamination is low. Now, an international panel of 35 allergy specialists, scientists, and patient advocates representing 21 countries, convened by the World Allergy Organization (WAO), is calling for an overhaul that would replace today’s confusing system with consistent, science-based rules.

    Today, shoppers face a confusing mix of precautionary allergen labeling phrases like “may contain,” “made in a facility with,” and “may contain traces.” The panel recommends replacing these variations with a single, straightforward statement: “May contain [allergen].” More importantly, manufacturers should not use these warnings simply as a precaution against lawsuits. Instead, companies should conduct formal risk assessments to determine whether unintended allergen contamination could expose consumers to amounts exceeding a scientifically established threshold. Warnings would generally be required only when that threshold could be exceeded.

    Click to visit sponsor

    To determine when a warning is necessary, the panel recommends using a scientific threshold known as ED05 (eliciting dose 5%). This represents the amount of allergenic protein estimated to trigger a reaction in approximately 5% of people with that particular allergy. The amount varies by allergen. For example, the reference dose is 2 milligrams of protein for peanuts, milk, and eggs, compared with 5 milligrams for wheat and fish. Rather than relying solely on concentrations measured in parts per million (ppm), the approach considers how much allergenic protein someone would actually consume in a typical serving. Importantly, ED05 is a statistical estimate, not a guarantee that the other 95% of allergic individuals will be safe.

    The ED05 threshold represents a somewhat practical compromise between protecting consumers and avoiding unnecessary warnings. If standards are set too strictly, manufacturers may feel compelled to place warnings on many products that pose little risk to most allergic consumers. When warnings become commonplace, shoppers may begin ignoring them, undermining their usefulness. The panel believes an ED05-based approach could make warnings more meaningful while maintaining a scientifically informed level of protection. However, the experts could not agree on how manufacturers should communicate the remaining risk to particularly sensitive consumers when allergen exposure falls below the warning threshold. Under the proposed system, a product without a “may contain” warning would not necessarily be safe for everyone with that allergy.

    The experts also took a clear stance on specialty food claims. If a package says a product is “free from” a specific allergen, 97% of the panel agreed that it should contain no detectable amount of that allergen, including accidental traces. Similarly, 80% supported changing the standard for “gluten-free” to require no detectable gluten, rather than allowing the small amounts currently permitted under regulations that set a limit of 20 parts per million. The panel also supported eliminating precautionary warnings for milk, eggs, and other animal-derived allergens on products labeled vegan. However, a vegan label does not guarantee that a product is free from accidental milk or egg contamination, so people with these allergies should not automatically assume vegan foods are safe.

    Click to visit sponsor

    To encourage manufacturers to adopt these science-based standards, the panel also addressed legal liability. Experts agreed that food companies demonstrating compliance with applicable food safety regulations should not be held legally responsible for allergic reactions caused by unintended allergen contamination. The goal is to reduce the incentive for manufacturers to place warnings on products simply to protect themselves from lawsuits. Instead, companies would have greater reason to conduct meaningful risk assessments and use warnings only when justified. These liability protections, like the other recommendations, are proposals rather than laws currently in effect.

    Ultimately, the recommendations are intended to help shape international food safety regulations as authorities work toward more consistent rules for allergen warnings. As lead researcher Antonio Bognanni, MD, PhD, of McMaster University, and colleagues explained, precautionary labeling “should only be applied when a legally regulated risk assessment indicates the likelihood of unintended allergen presence, which can pose a risk to allergic individuals.” The proposed changes could make grocery shopping clearer and less frustrating for families managing food allergies, but they would not eliminate the risk of allergic reactions. For consumers, the challenge will be understanding what the new warnings mean—and, just as importantly, what the absence of a warning does not guarantee.

    What do you think of these recommendations? Let us know in the comments section below. We will follow up in the coming days with our own take.

    Source: WAO Delphi Consensus Endorses ED05-Based Allergen Labelling — HCP Live

      1. Dena Friedel 2026/10/15 At 7:30 am

        This actually scares me more. Even though the labeling is not consistent, we can make our own decision of what level of risk we are willing to take or just be safe and avoid it all.

        If they set an arbitrary level that still may not be safe for everyone, this choice has been taken away and even more fear will exist for those with a history of anaphylaxis from trace allergens.

        I think they can do better for our community. Being afraid to eat, something we have to do to live, is a horrible way to live in this world that everything revolves around food.

        Reply
      2. Stephen Okon 2026/10/15 At 12:19 pm

        This misses the point, in my opinion. I care more about an unintended ingestion of an allergen, and much less about missing out on some product because of an overly aggressive/unnecessary “may contain” label.

        My understanding of the above is that their aim is to decrease the amount of unnecessary “may contain” or “made in….” statements that are placed on labels only to protect the manufacturer, even if there is really no suspicion for cross-contact/contamination. And therefore consumers with allergies would unnecessarily exclude those items from their diet.

        As a father of a child with allergies, that should NOT be the major goal or standardizing labeling practices. Of course, I don’t love excluding products from my purchases unnecessarily. But I’m MUCH MORE concerned about ingesting an unsuspected allergen.

        Many companies disclose “‘may contain” or facility information on their labels, but many do not.

        So when there is no “may contain” or “facility” on the label, I just don’t know if the product is made in a way that would be safe for my child , or not.

        Some companies have websites that clear this up, and others do not. Some have websites that you allow you to submit a question, and some answer those questions…and some do not. Some have costumer service phone lines or that are helpful…and some do not.

        So for me, the goal would be:

        1. continue “contains” statements, as is currently the stan.dard
        2. have companies – as a mandated standard – include a “may contains” statement when there is a risk for cross contact/contamination (I defer to those experts referenced above with regards to the threshold for that risk).

        Then, if there were no “may contain” statement, I would potentially feel safe with the product, without multiple attempts to contact a company to find out their individual manufacturing or labeling policies.

        Reply
